lesson.title: Building Dictionaries in One Line
lesson.summary: A dictionary comprehension builds a new dict from an iterable in a single expression, the same way a list comprehension builds a list.
lesson.body:
You have already seen how a list comprehension, like [x * x for x in range(5)], builds a whole new list in one compact line instead of a multi-line for loop with append calls. A dictionary comprehension applies that exact same idea to dictionaries, with one adjustment: instead of a single expression for each element, you write two expressions separated by a colon, one for the key and one for the value.

The general pattern is {key_expression: value_expression for item in iterable}, and just like a list comprehension, you can tack an if condition on the end to filter which items make it in.

words = ["apple", "kiwi", "banana", "fig"]
lengths = {word: len(word) for word in words}
print(lengths)

This prints {'apple': 5, 'kiwi': 4, 'banana': 6, 'fig': 3}. For every word in the list, the comprehension uses the word itself as the key and its length as the value, building all four entries in a single expression with no manual loop or empty dictionary to start from.

long_words = {w: l for w, l in lengths.items() if l > 4}
print(long_words)

This prints {'apple': 5, 'banana': 6}. Here the comprehension loops over lengths.items(), unpacking each (key, value) tuple into w and l exactly the way you would in a regular for loop, then keeps only the pairs where the length is greater than 4. 'kiwi' has length 4, which fails the strict greater than check, and 'fig' has length 3, so both are left out, while 'apple' and 'banana' make it through.

Dictionary comprehensions are most worth using when you are transforming or filtering an existing dictionary, or building a new one from some other iterable, in a way that is simple enough to read in one line. If the logic needs several steps or is hard to follow packed onto one line, a regular for loop is still the better, more readable choice.
